register: wave-4 authoring register (S-B4 tranche) — part 1 of 2

items.stem: State what a binary ionic compound contains, and name the classic example given in the note.
items.modelAnswer: A binary ionic compound contains just two elements joined by ionic bonding; the classic example is lead(II) bromide.

items.stem: State which substance is always the product at the cathode and which is always the product at the anode, when a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed.
items.modelAnswer: The cathode product is always the metal, and the anode product is always the non-metal.

items.stem: Explain why solid lead(II) bromide cannot be electrolysed, and what heating it past its melting point changes.
items.modelAnswer: In the solid the ions are held in place, but heated beyond its melting point the compound becomes molten and its ions can move freely, so the melt can conduct and electrolysis can happen.

items.stem: During the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide a grey solid forms on one electrode and a brown gas bubbles off the other. Identify both products and state the electrode at which each appears.
items.modelAnswer: The grey solid is lead, deposited at the cathode; the brown gas is bromine, given off at the anode.

items.stem: Name the two ions produced when water molecules split in an aqueous solution undergoing electrolysis.
items.modelAnswer: Water molecules split into H+ ions and OH- ions, which join the ions from the dissolved compound.

items.stem: State what is produced at the cathode when the dissolved metal is more reactive than hydrogen, and what is produced there when it is less reactive.
items.modelAnswer: Hydrogen forms at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; otherwise the metal itself is deposited there.

items.stem: A solution contains bromide ions. Explain which substance forms at the anode during its electrolysis, and why that substance rather than oxygen.
items.modelAnswer: A halide ion present at the anode is discharged to form the halogen, so bromine forms; the halide is discharged in preference to the OH- ions, so oxygen is not the product here.

items.stem: A solution contains ions of an unknown metal Z that sits below hydrogen in the reactivity series, and it contains no halide ions. Predict the product at each electrode.
items.modelAnswer: At the cathode the metal Z deposits, because a metal less reactive than hydrogen is discharged instead of hydrogen; at the anode oxygen forms from the OH- ions, because no halide is present to be discharged.

items.stem: Describe how a dot-and-cross diagram distinguishes the outer electrons of the two atoms in an ionic bond.
items.modelAnswer: Each atom's outer electrons are given their own symbol: dots for one atom and crosses for the other, so the two sets stay distinguishable in the drawing.

items.stem: Describe the finishing touch a correct ionic dot-and-cross diagram adds around each ion.
items.modelAnswer: Large square brackets enclose each ion, with the charge written outside at the top right in superscript.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of outer shells, why gaining one electron completes the chlorine atom's outer shell in the sodium chloride diagram.
items.modelAnswer: Chlorine is a Group 7 non-metal, so gaining the one electron that sodium loses completes its own outer shell; with one more electron than protons the ion carries a 1- charge.

items.stem: A dot-and-cross diagram is drawn for potassium fluoride, formed from a Group 1 metal and a Group 7 non-metal. Using the sodium chloride pattern, state how many electrons transfer and what each ion's charge is.
items.modelAnswer: One electron transfers: the potassium atom loses its single outer electron to reach a full outer shell, becoming a 1+ ion, and the fluorine atom gains that electron, becoming a 1- ion.

items.stem: State how many outer electrons a magnesium atom has available to give away, and which group provides that number.
items.modelAnswer: A magnesium atom has two outer electrons to give away, because magnesium sits in Group 2.

items.stem: State the charges of the two ions formed in magnesium oxide and the formula that follows from them.
items.modelAnswer: The ions formed are Mg2+ and O2-, and the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.

items.stem: Explain why the oxygen atom in magnesium oxide needs exactly two electrons from the magnesium atom.
items.modelAnswer: Oxygen sits in Group 6, so an oxygen atom needs two more electrons to complete its outer shell; both transferred electrons are received by the oxygen atom, filling it.

items.stem: A student draws the magnesium oxide diagram but shows one transferred electron coming from the oxygen atom. Using the transfer rule of record, correct the diagram and justify the correction.
items.modelAnswer: Both transferred electrons come from the magnesium atom, and both are received by the oxygen atom; the drawing must show both electrons as magnesium's electrons moving to the oxygen outer shell.

items.stem: Describe the melting behaviour and the building blocks of substances with giant covalent structures.
items.modelAnswer: They are solids that melt at high temperatures, built from huge numbers of non-metal atoms bonded to other non-metal atoms.

items.stem: Name the two standard examples of giant covalent structures given in the note.
items.modelAnswer: Diamond and graphite are the two standard examples of giant covalent structures.

items.stem: Explain why a giant covalent structure has a high melting point, referring to the bonds that must be overcome.
items.modelAnswer: High melting points follow because the strong covalent bonds run throughout the whole structure, and those bonds need lots of energy to overcome before the solid melts.

items.stem: A data booklet lists a solid as a 'giant lattice' of one non-metal element with a fixed atom ratio. Using the vocabulary of record, classify its structure type and state what is fixed about its composition.
items.modelAnswer: It is a giant covalent structure, also called a giant lattice; the ratio of atoms overall is fixed, even though huge numbers of atoms are bonded together.

items.stem: State the term for substances made of the same carbon atoms arranged in different bonding patterns, and name the two in this note.
items.modelAnswer: They are allotropes: diamond and graphite are both made of carbon atoms arranged in different bonding patterns.

items.stem: State how many other carbon atoms each carbon bonds to in graphite, and what structure those bonds build.
items.modelAnswer: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, forming layers of hexagons, and one electron per atom is left free.

items.stem: Explain why graphite is soft and slippery, and why it conducts electricity, in terms of its layers and electrons.
items.modelAnswer: Graphite is soft and slippery because its layers slide over each other, and it conducts because its delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.

items.stem: A workshop needs a material to cut through stone. Using diamond's bonding arrangement, justify which property makes it suitable and link it to its structure.
items.modelAnswer: Diamond is very hard, which makes it useful for cutting tools; the hardness follows from each carbon bonding to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement with very strong bonds.

items.stem: State what the atoms in a metal lattice become after releasing their outer electrons.
items.modelAnswer: Within the lattice the atoms lose their outer electrons, becoming positive metal ions.

items.stem: Describe the two features a drawn metallic lattice displays in two dimensions.
items.modelAnswer: It shows rows of positive ions with the delocalised electrons between them.

items.stem: Explain what the metallic bond is, naming the two players that attract each other inside the lattice.
items.modelAnswer: The metallic bond is the strong pull that the positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons exert on each other; that mutual attraction holds the lattice together.

items.stem: A circuit is connected to two terminals pressed onto a pure metal bar. Using the lattice model, explain what carries the current through the bar.
items.modelAnswer: The released outer electrons are delocalised and move freely between the positive ions, so these mobile electrons carry the current through the metal bar.

items.stem: State which forces must be broken when a metal melts, and what supplies the energy needed.
items.modelAnswer: Most metals have high melting and boiling points because strong electrostatic forces need lots of energy to break.

items.stem: State the term that describes a metal that can be hammered into shape.
items.modelAnswer: Such a metal is malleable, meaning it can be hammered into shape.

items.stem: Explain why a metal can be hammered into shape, in terms of the arrangement of its ions.
items.modelAnswer: Malleability works because the atoms or ions form layers, and a push makes one layer slide across its neighbour without breaking the structure apart.

items.stem: An overhead power line made of copper must carry current over a long distance. Using the bonding picture, state which particles carry the current and why copper is suited to this role.
items.modelAnswer: The delocalised electrons carry the current: metals conduct because their delocalised electrons are available to move and carry charge, so a copper wire lets its electron sea drift along the line.

items.stem: State the overall charge of every ionic compound, and how the ion charges relate to produce it.
items.modelAnswer: Ionic compounds carry no overall charge: the positive and negative charges on their ions cancel exactly.

items.stem: State the formula of iron(II) sulfate, given that the sulfate ion carries a 2- charge and the iron(II) ion a 2+ charge.
items.modelAnswer: One sulfate ion, carrying 2-, exactly cancels the 2+ charge on the iron(II) ion, so the formula is FeSO4.

items.stem: Explain the difference between saying an ionic compound is neutral and saying an atom is neutral.
items.modelAnswer: The neutrality belongs to the compound as a whole: its positive and negative ion charges cancel exactly, whereas a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons in one single particle — the two statements are not the same.

items.stem: Aluminium oxide is built from Al3+ ions and O2- ions. Using the direct comparison method of record, work out the formula and justify the ion counts.
items.modelAnswer: The charges are not equal in size, so more than one of each ion is needed: 2 x 3+ = 6+ from two aluminium ions cancels 3 x 2- = 6- from three oxide ions, giving the formula Al2O3.

items.stem: Describe the swap-and-drop rule for building an ionic formula from two ion charges.
items.modelAnswer: Swap-and-drop turns each ion's charge number into the other ion's count: as Cu2+ with Cl- gives CuCl2.

items.stem: State what is done with the positive and negative signs during swap-and-drop, and how a count of 1 is handled.
items.modelAnswer: Positive and negative signs are dropped during the method, and a count of 1 is never written.

items.stem: Explain why applying swap-and-drop to Ca2+ and S2- must not stop at Ca2S2, and what the correct formula is.
items.modelAnswer: With same-charge ions the method overcounts, so the resulting ratio must be reduced to its simplest whole numbers; Ca2S2 reduces to CaS, the correct formula of calcium sulfide.

items.stem: Magnesium hydroxide forms from Mg2+ ions and OH- ions. Apply swap-and-drop, and explain why brackets appear in the final formula.
items.modelAnswer: The 2+ charge swaps to give two hydroxide groups, and because the whole OH- group is doubled the formula is written Mg(OH)2 with the group inside brackets.

items.stem: Contrast the bonding inside a simple molecule with the forces between its neighbouring molecules.
items.modelAnswer: Simple molecular structures have strong covalent bonds inside each molecule but weak forces between neighbouring molecules.

items.stem: State the composition and shape of a C60 fullerene molecule as given in the note.
items.modelAnswer: C60 fullerene is a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms, joining 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons like a football.

items.stem: Explain why a simple molecular substance melts at a low temperature, naming what is overcome when it melts.
items.modelAnswer: The weak intermolecular forces between neighbouring molecules need only a little energy to overcome, so melting and boiling points are low; when the substance melts it is these weak forces that are overcome, not the strong covalent bonds.

items.stem: A student claims C60 fullerene should conduct electricity because it contains covalent bonds to many neighbours. Assess the claim using the electron behaviour of record.
items.modelAnswer: The claim is wrong: C60 cannot conduct, because its spare electrons move only within each buckyball and cannot migrate between the molecules, so no charge can travel through the solid.

items.stem: State what happens to the melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances as their relative molecular mass increases.
items.modelAnswer: Melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances rise as the relative molecular mass increases.

items.stem: Name the everyday insulating materials listed in the note.
items.modelAnswer: Common insulators include the plastic coating on household wiring, rubber and wood.

items.stem: Explain why a bigger simple molecule needs more heat before it changes state.
items.modelAnswer: Bigger molecules contain more electrons, so more intermolecular forces of attraction must be overcome; more intermolecular forces mean more heat energy is needed to change state, raising the melting and boiling points.

items.stem: A plug cover is made of plastic rather than metal. Using the particle behaviour of record, explain why the plastic keeps the user safe from shock.
items.modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are poor conductors because no free ions or mobile electrons exist to carry the charge, so the plastic cover does not let the current reach the user.
